transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-08-09
Start: 14:30 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Marcus Chen (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Redwood CSM), Jared Morales (Cerulean Head of Platform), Aisha Khan (Cerulean SRE), Tom Bender (Cerulean Security), Maya Rivera (Cerulean Product)

Summary:
Follow-up on the 2027-08-03 production incident where Cerulean observed elevated latency and KV cache thrash during a traffic spike. Review of root cause, mitigations applied, and next steps for reliability improvements and a proposed pilot/benchmark.

Transcript:
[00:00] Lena Park: thanks everyone for joining, i know we have a short window so we'll try to be focused. quick roll call?
[00:12] Jared Morales: Jared here, hey.
[00:14] Aisha Khan: Aisha on the SRE team.
[00:17] Tom Bender: Tom from security.
[00:19] Maya Rivera: Maya, product.
[00:21] Marcus Chen: Marcus, systems eng on redwood.
[00:23] Priya Rao: Priya, CSM. thanks.
[00:25] Lena Park: ok quick goal: validate RCA, confirm mitigations, align on pilot and runbook changes, and owners. Marcus, can you walk us through the technical postmortem notes?
[00:40] Marcus Chen: yeah sure. so root cause they saw was cache thrashing on the KV cache layer in the serving runtime during the spike. basically we had an unusual sequence length distribution and a sudden increase in parallel sessions which resulted in a lot of KV evictions and thus more cold-start decode work. that combined with a misconfigured autoscale policy on the customer's dedicated pool — threshold was too high — so new workers were slow to come up and the per-token latency spiked.
[01:15] Marcus Chen: additionally we found that the model variant used was not quantization-optimized for that batch size, so some kernels on the GPU fell back to less-efficient paths. small point: logs showed a short period where the fallback to a smaller model variant didn't trigger because model routing policy matched exact model id only.
[01:40] Aisha Khan: can you clarify "kv cache thrash" — are we talking eviction because of memory pressure or TTL?
[01:48] Marcus Chen: mostly memory pressure + ephemeral sessions. the traffic pattern opened many short-lived chats that didn't benefit from prefix caching; the KV growth exceeded the preset per-node cache budget and evicted older entries. then those older entries were needed which forced recompute.
[02:10] Maya Rivera: that matches what product saw: lots of small chat sessions from the new onboarding flow, high concurrency. we hadn't anticipated so many simultaneous cold users.
[02:22] Jared Morales: timeline question — when did autoscale lag begin?
[02:25] Marcus Chen: scaling lag started ~14:02 UTC, about three minutes after the spike began. the autoscaler was configured with a 120s cool-down plus a high CPU threshold so it didn't add nodes until we hit sustained pressure.
[02:42] Tom Bender: from the security side, any data-plane impact? did any logs indicate token leakage or PII exposure?
[02:50] Marcus Chen: no evidence of data leakage; all storage was encrypted and KV entries are ephemeral runtime blobs. we did see an increase in error-rate (5xx) for a ~7 minute window but those were timeouts/rejected requests, not content leakage.
[03:08] Lena Park: ok good. Priya, you mentioned a mitigation you pushed last week?
[03:13] Priya Rao: yes, we coordinated a mitigation: temporarily increased the cache budget per node, lowered the autoscale cooldown to 30s for their Dedicated pool, and enabled an immediate model-variant fallback rule that allows fallback on batch-size mismatch. we also added a short-term request queue to smooth bursts. the customer applied those at 16:30 UTC on 2027-08-04 and latency improved back near baseline.
[03:42] Aisha Khan: we measured P95 down from 1.8s to 420ms after the changes, so that's good. but we're worried about long term — if a bigger spike hits, will that hold?
[03:55] Marcus Chen: long term we recommend a couple things: 1) a pre-warmed buffer of warm workers for their Dedicated pool during onboarding campaigns, 2) KV sharding improvements and soft-ttl for ephemeral sessions, 3) smarter routing policy that can route noisy short chats to a cheaper, smaller model variant, and 4) a canary and gradual rollout policy for model/quantization changes.
[04:20] Jared Morales: is pre-warm something redwood can automate? like scheduled pre-warm based on campaign start times or traffic predictions?
[04:28] Marcus Chen: yes we have scheduling hooks. we can provision a pre-warmed buffer and also integrate with their campaign scheduler — we can trigger a warm-up job via an API call. we'll propose a simple workflow for pilot.
[04:38] Maya Rivera: on soft-ttl — how aggressive is that? we don't want stale context to persist and cause hallucinations.
[04:45] Marcus Chen: good point. soft-ttl recommendation is to keep ephemeral sessions for 30s-2m depending on session pattern, and to drop any user history beyond X tokens when routing to the smaller variant. also implement quality checks that if the model context is trimmed, we don't escalate to product for false positives — basically instrument prompts so we can audit quality regression.
[05:10] Tom Bender: on encryption and KMS — you said storage is encrypted. do you offer customer-managed keys (CMK) for dedicated/private?
[05:18] Lena Park: yes, for Dedicated and Private deployments we support KMS/HSM integrations; we'll share our KMS docs. Priya, can you add that to action items?
[05:26] Priya Rao: noted. I'll share SOC2 + KMS docs and network diagram.
[05:30] Jared Morales: thanks. about the fallback policy — earlier you said fallback was exact model-id match. can you make it more flexible like semantic compatibility?
[05:39] Marcus Chen: we can. the routing layer supports compatibility tiers — we'll configure a fallback that matches architecture family and quantization level, not only exact id. there is a small risk of quality delta; we'll tie that to post-deploy evaluations.
[05:55] Aisha Khan: for instrumentation, what metrics should we capture during the pilot?
[05:58] Marcus Chen: minimal set: P50/P95/P99 latency, 5xx error rate, KV cache hit rate, worker spin-up time, GPU utilization, and model variant fallback count. also token-level cost per request so you can watch economics.
[06:12] Lena Park: and we'll put a dashboard in the console with alerts at thresholds.
[06:16] Marcus Chen: yes. we'll create a per-route dashboard and add alerting rules.
[06:20] Maya Rivera: about the pilot: what success metrics does redwood want and what do we define as success?
[06:26] Lena Park: two-sided. for Cerulean we expect P95 under 600ms for 99% of pilot windows and 5xx < 0.5%. Redwood wants to validate autoscale responsiveness and KV cache stability under a 3x synthetic spike. so success = meet latency/error targets while keeping cost within 1.5x baseline.
[06:50] Jared Morales: that seems fair. timeline — we want this soon, the next onboarding campaign is 2027-08-16. can pilot be in the week prior?
[06:58] Marcus Chen: we can start config and baseline tests 2027-08-12, run synthetic spike tests 8/14-8/15, and if all good enable pilot to run during campaign starting 8/16.
[07:10] Tom Bender: security checklist — we'll need an updated network diagram and proof of encryption-in-transit and at-rest, plus any SOC2 artefacts. also need a contract amendment for dedicated buffer usage.
[07:24] Priya Rao: we'll attach the SOC2 report and KMS docs, and legal will produce an amendment template.
[07:30] Jared Morales: regarding logs — we need to keep more verbose logs for two weeks for post-incident analysis. is that ok re: cost?
[07:36] Lena Park: we can increase retention for pilot, we'll flag that as temporary and provide an estimate of storage cost.
[07:41] Aisha Khan: one operational ask: can we get a playbook that maps specific incident patterns to remediation steps? like if KV eviction rate > X then increase cache budget by Y or shard by Z.
[07:53] Marcus Chen: yes, we have runbook templates. we'll produce a Cerulean-specific playbook with threshold-based actions and runbook runbooks for on-call.
[08:02] Maya Rivera: can you include guidance for when to shift traffic to a cheaper model variant automatically? that's a product-level decision too.
[08:09] Marcus Chen: we'll include a recommended policy and escape hatch: automatic shift on high latency for N minutes, with immediate rollback conditions if quality checks fail.
[08:19] Jared Morales: on monitoring — do you support distributed tracing into model kernels? we'd like to see where time is spent (tokenization, attention, kernel fallback).
[08:28] Marcus Chen: we expose spans for request lifecycle, and for GPU kernels we provide sampled metrics. full tracing into kernel internals is limited but we can provide aggregated stage timings.
[08:40] Aisha Khan: what's the expected time to carry out the KV sharding work? if we need code changes to runtime, how long?
[08:47] Marcus Chen: some sharding improvements are configuration only and can be done in days; deeper runtime changes would be on a 4–8 week engineering cadence. for the pilot we'll stick to config-level soft-ttl and per-route cache tuning.
[09:00] Lena Park: ok let's recap owners and deadlines. Marcus on logs/export + KV snapshots due 8/12; Priya on SOC2/KMS docs due 8/11; Jared to confirm pilot scope and metrics by 8/13. Redwood to set up pre-warm buffer API integration by 8/15.
[09:18] Jared Morales: confirmed.
[09:20] Tom Bender: quick question on canary config: will we be able to control percentage and rollback thresholds?
[09:26] Marcus Chen: yes you can set canary percentages, automatic rollback on metric regressions, and manual promote when ready.
[09:32] Maya Rivera: about cost — if we pre-warm, do we pay for those warm workers even if idle?
[09:38] Lena Park: yes it's reserved capacity charges; we'll model cost and propose a commitment level for the pilot.
[09:44] Aisha Khan: any recommendations to reduce cost while keeping reliability?
[09:47] Marcus Chen: use cheaper smaller model variant for cold short chats, enable prefix caching when sessions become long-lived, and use autoscale with fast ramp for temporary spikes. also token-level batching where possible.
[09:58] Jared Morales: one last security question: for Dedicated pool, are audit logs forwarded to our SIEM?
[10:04] Priya Rao: yes we support forwarding to common SIEMs via syslog and can set up an ETL for the fields you need.
[10:11] Tom Bender: great.
[10:13] Lena Park: alright, let's finalize next steps — Marcus will send logs and a short benchmark plan, Priya will share docs and runbook template, legal will draft amendment, and we'll aim to start synthetic tests on 8/14.
[10:27] Marcus Chen: i'll include the KV cache hit-rate graphs and a proposed config change set in the notes.
[10:32] Priya Rao: i'll upload SOC2 summary and KMS integration doc to the shared drive and post link.
[10:36] Jared Morales: please also include the expected cost delta for a 2-hour pre-warm buffer at 2x baseline.
[10:42] Lena Park: will do. any final questions?
[10:44] Maya Rivera: none from product.
[10:46] Aisha Khan: no.
[10:48] Tom Bender: all good.
[10:50] Lena Park: thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the links and items by the dates noted.

References / shared artifacts:
- Benchmark spreadsheet (Marcus to share): link: https://redwood.example.com/benchmarks/cerulean-08-2027 (internal)
- SOC2 summary + KMS doc (Priya to share): placeholder link: https://redwood.example.com/security/cerulean-kms-soc2
- Runbook template: https://redwood.example.com/runbooks/kv-cache-playbook

Closing notes:
Customer is willing to run pilot ahead of campaign provided Redwood delivers logs and config changes within the week. Key risks: larger-than-expected spike exposing deeper runtime changes; quality regression when routing to smaller variants. Mitigations: phased pilot, canary traffic, post-deploy evals.
